title: Why physicists drove a trap full of antimatter through traffic on a truck
excerpt: Physicists drove 92 antiprotons around CERN on a truck without losing one – a first step toward quieter antimatter labs.
content:
Physicists drove 92 antiprotons around CERN on a truck without losing one – a first step toward quieter antimatter labs.

Antimatter doesn’t last long in our world. When an antiproton meets ordinary matter, the two destroy each other in a burst of energy. Yet in March, physicists loaded 92 antiprotons onto a truck and drove them 4.7 miles (7.5 kilometers) in regular traffic. Every one of them came back.

Nobody had moved antiprotons by road before. For the team, the drive shows that precise antimatter experiments could one day leave the building where their antiprotons are made.

The drive was the work of the BASE collaboration, led by Stefan Ulmer and Christian Smorra of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany. It was a short trip, two laps of a loop inside CERN, the physics laboratory near Geneva better known for its particle colliders. But it answered the question the team’s plan depended on.

Lab noise limits the measurements

Every particle of ordinary matter has an antimatter twin with the opposite electric charge. BASE compares protons with antiprotons, measuring how much each weighs relative to its charge and how strongly each behaves like a tiny magnet.

If the twins show even tiny differences, that could help explain why the universe is made of matter at all. In the early universe, the two should have formed in equal amounts and destroyed each other.

BASE has already compared the two particles’ charge-to-mass ratios with an uncertainty of 16 parts per trillion. Its magnetism measurement for antiprotons carries an uncertainty of 1.6 parts per billion. So far, the twins haven’t differed in either one.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ulmer described what the team hopes the comparisons could turn up. “Maybe we will find some interesting clue on why there is matter/antimatter symmetry on laboratory scales, but not on cosmological scales,” he said.

Until now, experiments like these could only run at CERN’s Antimatter Factory, where the antiprotons are made. Running the facility makes the magnetic field around the experiment fluctuate, and that now limits BASE’s precision. Ulmer compared it to studying something through a very powerful microscope while someone shakes it.

Building a trap that travels

To hold antimatter, a trap has to keep it away from everything, including air. The trap, called BASE-STEP, holds charged particles inside a near-perfect vacuum using a strong magnetic field and a carefully shaped electric field.

The magnet is superconducting and runs at about minus 452°F (4.3 kelvin). Liquid helium and a cooling machine keep it there.

The apparatus weighs about 1,870 pounds (850 kilograms) and fits on a steel frame. For the trip, the team lowered the magnet’s field to reduce the risk that it would suddenly stop superconducting. They also cut the frame off from the lab’s power and cooling.

Batteries ran the electronics. An overhead crane lifted the frame onto a medium-duty truck, whose bed held an 11,000-pound (5-metric-ton) steel plate to soften bumps and vibration.

No antiprotons were lost on the road

The team had already moved protons this way in 2024, in a trial run with the same trap. On March 24, the antiproton truck drove two laps of a 2.2-mile (3.5-kilometer) loop across CERN’s main site. It took 24 minutes, with a top speed of about 25 miles per hour (40.8 kilometers per hour).

Asked by Earth.com about the most nerve-wracking moment, Ulmer said it was the road trip itself. The open question was “whether the vacuum will remain good enough during the transport, such that the particles will not annihilate due to pressure increase caused by transport-induced vibrations,” he said.

A detector wired to the trap picks up a faint electrical signal from the trapped cloud, and it recorded that signal every minute of the ride. The size of the signal depends on how many antiprotons are inside.

Measured over a full day before and after the trip, the signal changed by less than a tenth of what losing a single antiproton would produce. None were lost.

The frame ran on its own for 2.72 hours, from unplugging to reconnection. In that time, about 3 gallons (11 liters) of liquid helium boiled away, nearly half the supply. The batteries used about half their charge.

The vacuum beat its own target

The team loaded the antiprotons on March 7 and kept watching them for 33 days. Stray gas atoms didn’t destroy a single one.

One antiproton was lost on day 26, during a test that split the cloud into two groups and merged it again. The team needs that control, because it plans to hand small batches of antiprotons to other experiments. The researchers managed to separate out as few as one.

From the lack of losses, the team calculated that the gas pressure inside the trap stayed below 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ millibar. The trap had been designed to reach 1 × 10⁻¹⁶ millibar, so the pressure was at least 45 times lower than planned.

As far as the authors know, that is the lowest pressure reported for a trap of this open design, one that lets particles in and out. They estimated that an antiproton in it would last at least seven years before a gas atom destroyed it.

The road to Düsseldorf

Eventually, BASE wants to drive antiprotons to quieter labs, including one being built at the university in Düsseldorf. There, the team expects measurements at least 100 times more precise than the Antimatter Factory allows.

Getting there means a much longer drive. Ulmer estimated the current apparatus could travel about 370 miles (600 kilometers) before its magnet stops superconducting as the cold liquids evaporate. The team’s goal is 500 miles (800 kilometers), using a truck with its own generator.

“Our next target is to make the trap sufficiently autonomous to allow a ten-hour transport from Geneva to Düsseldorf,” Smorra said.

Other steps come first. The antiprotons have to be moved from the traveling trap into a waiting experiment, which BASE hasn’t done yet. The team also wants to carry bigger clouds, up to about 1,000 antiprotons, and that will need an upgraded trap.

Whether protons and antiprotons differ at all is still an open question. The team plans to keep looking, in a quieter lab.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.
